question: Tell me about his payments work.
raw_text:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work across **JP Morgan Chase**, **American Express**, and **RBC**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt was Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation. The underlying WebSeries platform needed custom engineering to support distinct payment formatting, validation, compliance, and workflows for **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. He managed a blended team of **40+** across Accenture and the bank, working directly with Bottomline Technologies at its Portsmouth offices.

Matt designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules. Rather than relying on out-of-box capabilities, he built payment-type-specific entitlements, Message Authentication Code security, contextual guidance, sanctions screening, and integration with centralized transaction monitoring. He also led the payments data migration from regional legacy systems, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011** as the bank’s unified global corporate banking portal.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform was replacing a legacy mainframe, but missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, and no sandbox were slowing adoption. Matt co-created a developer portal with Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, use case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. He introduced environment virtualization for earlier testing, used Lean Product and XP practices, and conducted a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch; onboarding time decreased. The portal team also exceeded its delivery commitment by **over 261 story points** of customer-focused value.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border payments. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, including real-time FX integration, automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and batch processing. The work produced a **complete implementation blueprint**, while revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays and improved SLA compliance.

question: What went wrong?
raw_text:
🐾 There were production defects—not just delivery complexity—on **JP Morgan Chase’s** ACCESS program.

One specific failure was in the Message Authentication Code (MAC) security layer, which let corporate users verify payment integrity before release. Matt used break-glass production access and SQL queries against live payment data to investigate. The root cause was **missing unit tests and weak error handling**. The account doesn’t specify how many payments or customers were affected, how long the incident lasted, or whether there was financial loss.

The rollout also exposed **data issues carried over from the legacy platform during migration**. Regional systems had different schemas, client configurations, entitlement structures, and transaction histories. Matt ran UAT and production validation/shakeout testing, then triaged defects that emerged after cutover. The migration itself was completed **without disruption to live payment operations**; that does not mean the rollout was defect-free.

These weren’t isolated from his delivery responsibilities. Matt repeatedly owned on-call and **Sev-1** incident response across releases, waves, and migrations. He coordinated root-cause analysis across the bank’s New York team, engineers in Mumbai and Bangalore, and Bottomline Technologies, while running status updates and daily leadership calls during live incidents.

The broader starting problem was that WebSeries’ out-of-box capabilities did not cover the bank’s payment, security, and workflow requirements. The gateway also had to replace fragmented integrations across **12 countries**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, but the stories explicitly record production failures and post-cutover defects along the way.

question: What’s his leadership style?
raw_text:
🐾 Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose.

At **Accenture**, Matt described inherited engineering teams as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” In the early Cloud Innovation Center, a rigid hierarchical culture made people slow to share ideas. Teams also avoided risks because they feared blame, contributing to slower delivery and missed opportunities.

Matt pushed decisions to the people closest to the work, made intent explicit, and used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He established weekly brainstorming sessions where ideas were considered without judgment. Rather than emphasizing individual accolades, he recognized contributions that advanced shared project goals.

His “permit to fail” environment included non-punitive post-mortems and lean, low-stakes experiments. Teams examined mistakes without pointing fingers and applied lessons to subsequent sprints. In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail—and treated those results as evidence for deciding what to build next, before committing to costly engineering work.

He also brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams. Coaching meant helping teams think clearly, not just execute tasks. Automation, continuous delivery, quality-first practices, and thin-slice, production-ready solutions gave those teams ways to test ideas and get user feedback.

Across leadership roles that included a **150-person** Cloud Innovation Center, Matt’s leadership-philosophy story reports **4x delivery acceleration** once teams embraced lean product and modern engineering practices. His teams also applied post-mortem lessons to prevent recurring failure patterns and shortened project timelines through controlled experimentation.

question: Give me an example where that didn’t work.
raw_text:
🐾 There’s an example where Matt took accountability, but the tester still faced the consequence.

In one global platform modernization engagement for a financial services client, Matt was the tech lead responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup across development, QA, UAT, and production. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across environments.

Matt relied on inherited documentation rather than verifying the IAM configuration, environment boundaries, and downstream access controls. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes. He also did not implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and worked collectively with the team on root cause analysis and remediation. But the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

This was not a controlled, low-stakes experiment within his “permit to fail” approach. It was a failure to verify safeguards he was responsible for. His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became “day-one leadership responsibilities” in his delivery approach.

question: Give me an example.
raw_text:
🐾 Here’s a concrete example from **Norfolk Southern**.

During the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement in **2020**, Matt’s team was modernizing **Norfolk Southern’s** legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, as the pandemic forced work fully remote, the client reported rising defects—even though the dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns reached both the client and **Accenture** account leadership.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He investigated and found that an engineer was building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete, but defects went undetected. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend test-driven development experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team, redoing code and test cases.

Instead of stopping at a process change, Matt organized hands-on coaching: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing with subject-matter experts using an “I do, we do, you do” progression. He also delivered product management and SMART story training.

Defect rates dropped as story quality and test-first discipline took hold. **The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.** Client confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement; the story does not report a numerical defect-reduction rate.

question: What’s his leadership style?
raw_text:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership: empathy, clarity, and purpose.

Many engineering teams he inherited were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, teams also faced hierarchical bottlenecks, silos between engineering, design, and product, and fear of blame when experiments failed. He made intent explicit, pushed decisions to the people closest to the work, and used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He coached teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks. Engineers, product managers, and UX architects worked in balanced teams with equal participation and shared accountability, rather than handing work from role to role. Pair programming, collaborative coding, stand-ups, and retrospectives made feedback part of daily work.

They delivered thin-slice, production-ready solutions to get user feedback instead of waiting for complete requirements.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams accelerated delivery **4x** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. Across the balanced-team engagements, teams reduced handoffs and project delays and achieved **zero-defect production code**. Post-mortem lessons were applied to subsequent sprints to prevent identified failure patterns from recurring.

question: Give me an example.
raw_text:
🐾 Here’s a specific example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In early **2020**, Matt’s Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the railroad’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A few months into the engagement, the client reported rising defects even though the team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and Accenture account leadership, just as the pandemic moved everyone to remote work.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite, then showed the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story and writing tests after the code. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done.

Instead of simply asking engineers to improve their coverage numbers, Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought in frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the team and redo the code and tests properly. Coaching followed an “I do, we do, you do” progression, supported by boot camps, coding katas, and practice learning sessions.

To keep those practices in place after the experts left, he made test creation a visible step before implementation, checked at standup. Pairs rotated daily, and newer engineers worked with seasoned practitioners. Remote pairs traded drivers frequently rather than abandoning pairing when co-location disappeared.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Client confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement. Pairing and test-first remained the team’s default after the experts went home, and the failure mode that caused the crisis did not recur.
